solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Dismiss — throw out abruptly and hire anew

indicators.note: cut off abruptly, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: to cast something is to throw it out

indicators.note: made anew, these four letters are put into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A boss sacks someone on the spot and then takes on a replacement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abruptly' cuts the last letter from CAST to leave CAS; 'anew' rearranges HIRE as HIER.
explanation.definitionFit: To cashier an officer is to dismiss them from the service in disgrace.

clue.text: Nick gets hit with limp

parts.note: to cop it is British slang for getting punished or hit, so one who gets hit cops
to hop is to move lamely on one foot

explanation.surface: A man is struck and walks off limping.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang 'nick' is both to arrest and a police station.
explanation.definitionFit: Nick is British slang for a police station, as is the informal compound.

clue.text: Putting on fifty, one gluing bandages — like this one?

definitions.text: Putting on fifty, one gluing bandages — like this one?

parts.note: to stick something somewhere is to put it there

indicators.note: the glue word wraps around the numeral like a dressing

parts.note: a paster is one who pastes or glues
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Someone applies fifty adhesive bandages, asking if this one is of that kind.
explanation.walkthrough: As a whole the clue describes sticking on an adhesive dressing.
explanation.definitionFit: An adhesive bandage is a small dressing glued over a wound, which the clue's picture shows.

clue.text: Prisoners keeping it up for friends

indicators.note: the prisoners word holds the reversed pair within it

parts.note: inmates are those held in a prison

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the small word is written bottom to top

explanation.surface: Jailed men keep their spirits up for the sake of their mates.
explanation.definitionFit: Intimates are close friends, people one is on familiar terms with.

clue.text: Game female meeting American king of old

parts.note: RU is rugby union

explanation.surface: A sporty woman meets an American and an old monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: William II of England was nicknamed for his ruddy face.
explanation.definitionFit: William II, the son of the Conqueror, was known by this nickname, so he is a historical monarch.

clue.text: Opposite directions taken in trail to get back

indicators.note: the two compass letters are taken into the trail word

parts.note: a spoor is the track or scent trail of an animal
north and south are opposite compass points, N and S

explanation.surface: Someone goes both ways along a path to retrace their steps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' looks like part of 'get back' (return), but it is a verb meaning support.
explanation.definitionFit: To back a person or venture is to support it, especially with money, as a sponsor does.

clue.text: Upset, sculptor is languishing — take stock from that

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset turns the whole phrase upside down

parts.note: Henry Moore was a celebrated English sculptor
one who languishes rots away

explanation.surface: An upset artist pines away and tells you to draw a lesson from it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' turns MOORE ROTS bottom to top. 'take stock' looks like reflect, but means fetch supplies.
explanation.definitionFit: A storeroom holds supplies, so it is the place one takes stock from.

clue.text: Too heavy, gong size at the limits

parts.note: gong is British slang for a medal or honour, such as the OBE (Order of the British Empire)

indicators.note: only the outermost letters of the word are kept

explanation.surface: A large gong is too heavy at its maximum size.
explanation.definitionFit: Obese means grossly overweight, heavier than is healthy.

clue.text: Jet carrying me home not designed to contain force, suddenly improvised

indicators.note: the jet word carries everything else inside it

parts.note: a spurt is a jet of liquid

indicators.note: the rearranged letters hold the force symbol
designed means newly arranged, so the three words are rearranged

parts.note: F is the symbol for force in physics

explanation.surface: A plane carrying someone home not built to withstand force, a hasty arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'designed' rearranges ME HOME NOT around F to give OFTHEMOMEN, which sits inside SPURT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done on impulse, without planning, is said to be done on the spur of the moment.

clue.text: Second in Premiership proves infuriating for Scottish team

indicators.note: only the second letter of the league's name is used

parts.note: something that angers people proves infuriating to them

explanation.surface: A Premiership side in second place infuriates a Scottish club.
explanation.walkthrough: Rangers is a Glasgow football club; the Premiership is a football league.
explanation.definitionFit: Glasgow Rangers is one of Scotland's best-known football clubs.

clue.text: Moment of truth is ace!

parts.note: an ace in tennis is a serve the opponent cannot hit back, a point with no return; the phrase also names the moment of commitment

explanation.surface: An excited cry that a moment of revelation is wonderful.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'ace' as the tennis serve: a point won where the ball is never sent back.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means the stage past which turning back is impossible, a decisive moment of truth.

clue.text: Smell engulfing less than brilliant sickly stuff

indicators.note: the smell word swallows the other piece whole

parts.note: hum is British slang for a bad smell
something merely OK is adequate but not brilliant

explanation.surface: A nasty odour surrounds some unappetising, sickly food.
explanation.definitionFit: Hokum is mawkish, sentimental or bogus material, the cloying stuff of melodrama.

clue.text: Bully ever so tired after dispensing with Irish docker

indicators.note: to bully is to push around, so the remaining letters are shoved into a new order
the Irish abbreviation is removed from the phrase before it is worked on

explanation.surface: A worn-out Irish dockworker is picked on by a bully.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing IR from EVER SO TIRED leaves EVERSOTED, which 'Bully' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: A stevedore is a labourer who loads and unloads ships in port.

clue.text: Particular joke, one getting fired after a setback in company

parts.note: a pun is a joke on words

indicators.note: the reversed pieces sit within the company abbreviation
a setback sends the pair of pieces into reverse order

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I
a fire that has been lit has been fired, set alight

explanation.surface: A worker tells a joke and then gets the sack after a setback at the firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after a setback' reverses one plus fired to give TILI; 'fired' looks like sacked but means set alight.
explanation.definitionFit: A punctilio is a fine point of etiquette, a particular or detail to be observed.

clue.text: Tough sailor about to be shelled in a storm

indicators.note: a storm tosses the letters into a new order
shelling removes the outer letters of the word

explanation.surface: A hardy seaman is about to come under shellfire during a storm.
explanation.walkthrough: Shelled ABOUT gives BOU; 'in a storm' mixes SAILOR and BOU. 'Tough' looks like describing the sailor, but means difficult.
explanation.definitionFit: Laborious work is tough, needing great effort, here in American spelling.

clue.text: Snacks, combining two placed in reverse

parts.note: bi- is the combining form meaning two, as in bicycle

indicators.note: the word for placed is read from right to left

parts.note: to set something is to place it

explanation.surface: A puzzle about snacks made by pairing two items and putting them back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: Bites are small mouthfuls of food, light snacks.

clue.text: Star — or moon for children?

definitions.meaning: an important person, a top dog
children are told the moon is made of cheese, a large round one

explanation.surface: Asks whether a celestial body is a star or the moon of nursery tales.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a self-important leading figure; literally a huge cheese, as the moon is in children's stories.

clue.text: Tea finally taken between typically hot and cold snacks

indicators.note: the letter is put in the middle of the taps word

parts.note: taps are the things labelled hot and cold over a sink

indicators.note: only the last letter of the drink is used

explanation.surface: A cup of tea is enjoyed between courses of hot and cold small dishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hot and cold' looks like it describes the snacks, but it defines TAPS.
explanation.definitionFit: Tapas are small Spanish savoury dishes served as snacks with drinks.

clue.text: There once dwelt with Gandhi conflict, though the anger all ending

indicators.note: the final letter of each of the seven words is taken

explanation.surface: Gandhi's people once lived with conflict, though all their anger ended.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic word means to that place, so it suits a definition marked as old usage.

clue.text: Go on then, I'd like to entertain you

definitions.meaning: a permissive phrase inviting someone to help themselves
a host's offer of hospitality to a visitor

explanation.surface: A host gives permission and offers hospitality.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase grants permission to go ahead, and is also a host's invitation to be entertained.

clue.text: Leaders in the ruck bearing down on player that's powerful on the field

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits on top of the player
the opening letter of each of the two words is taken

parts.note: an actor is a player on stage

explanation.surface: Rugby forwards in a ruck push down on an opponent, a powerful presence on the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a rugby pitch; the field is farmland.
explanation.definitionFit: A tractor is a powerful farm vehicle used to work the fields.

clue.text: First in month, then flower appearing

parts.note: Aug is the abbreviation for August
a flower is something that flows, here the Ural, a Russian river

explanation.surface: A flower blooms early in the month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' is crosswordese for a river (a thing that flows), here the Ural.
explanation.definitionFit: An inaugural event is the first of its kind, marking an opening or beginning.

clue.text: Cupidity OK having skimmed off capital

indicators.note: the capital, the opening letter, is removed

parts.note: saying OK means it is agreed

explanation.surface: Greed is approved once someone has creamed off the money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' looks like money, but means the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Cupidity is a strong desire for wealth or possessions, i.e. avarice.

clue.text: Plant plenty around base of plateau

indicators.note: the plenty word goes around the single letter

parts.note: lots means plenty

indicators.note: in a down clue the base is the final letter

explanation.surface: Plenty of greenery grows around the foot of a plateau.
explanation.definitionFit: The lotus is a water lily, a sacred plant in Asia.

clue.text: Uproar with cries of excitement, one way or the other?

indicators.note: the cries are read the other way, from right to left

parts.note: ah and ooh are excited exclamations

explanation.surface: A noisy fuss of excited shouting, whichever way it goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one way or the other' turns AH OOH round to read right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoo-ha is a commotion or fuss, an uproar over something.

clue.text: Bite and howl when beaten — corporal punishment gets to deliver a mean blow

indicators.note: beaten like eggs, the two words are mixed up

parts.note: a beating with a leather strap was a traditional school punishment

explanation.surface: Someone bites and howls while being thrashed, punished with a leather strap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when beaten' rearranges BITE and HOWL into HITBELOW.
explanation.definitionFit: The boxing idiom for an illegal low punch means acting unfairly or cruelly.

clue.text: Screen in episode rerun backwards

indicators.note: backwards says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A television episode is shown again on the screen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' marks the letters held inside 'episode rerun'; 'backwards' reads them right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: A reredos is an ornamental screen behind a church altar.

clue.text: Top Cornish apple?

parts.note: Cornwall is in the South West of England, abbreviated SW
an eater is an eating apple, as opposed to a cooker

explanation.surface: Asks about the best apple from Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' looks like an adjective praising the apple, but it is a garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweater is a knitted pullover, a top worn on the upper body.
